\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440\cf1\f0\fs24 Council President Bethea opened the public hearing at 4:10 PM.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 Growth Management Director Jeff Shrum presented Ordinance 2026-5, an applicant-initiated text amendment to Chapter 122 of the City Code to allow aboveground air curtain incinerators as an ancillary use by right at materials recovery facilities citywide. The amendment establishes criteria including a minimum 10-acre site, compliance with all federal, state, and local regulations, setbacks, hours of operation, an operations plan, residue removal, storage limits, and annual fire permits with daily burn approvals. Additional provisions address enforcement, annual compliance reviews, and authority for immediate cessation of operations for safety concerns. The ordinance applies to all qualifying facilities, with Friends Recycling currently meeting the acreage requirement. Two other properties \par
\par
Mr. Shrum noted that the Planning Commission recommended approval on November 10, 2025, and the proposal was presented at the Governor\rquote s meeting on November 18 with no objections. Staff recommends approval, stating that mitigation measures were incorporated to address potential impacts. He reminded this is a legislative hearing, and options include approving, revising, or denying the ordinance, and requested if Council had revisions, that Growth and Legal staff be allowed time to review to avoid unintended consequences.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield asked for clarification on the usage of air curtain incinerators on construction sites. Mr. Shrum explained that this ordinance only applies to materials recovery facilities (MRFs); State law permits the usage of mobile air curtain incinerators on construction sites. He further explained the location of air curtain incinerators within a MRF would be determined on a site plan, and would not be allowed to be moved around the property. Additionally, it would only be allowed as an ancillary use to a MRF, which has a Chapter 163 Developer\rquote s Agreement requirement. \par
\par
Fred Roberts, attorney for the applicant, 40 SE 11th Avenue, explained the purpose of the application to amend the code, noting that current ordinances are silent on air curtain incinerators, though open burning is permitted under Florida Forestry Service regulations. He stated the proposed use would allow vegetative debris from multiple sites to be processed at a single location, providing an environmentally sensitive, sustainable, and cleaner alternative to chipping and grinding. Mr. Roberts emphasized that air curtain incinerators reduce smoke and emissions by burning at high temperatures and recirculating byproducts, and that the proposed ordinance includes extensive safeguards such as site plan and operational plan requirements, industrial performance standards, annual city review, setbacks, and daily ignition approvals. Oversight would involve the City of Ocala, FDEP air quality permitting, Florida Forestry Service, and EPA standards. He noted the equipment is highly regulated and the ordinance sets a high compliance bar, ensuring robust protections. \par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 Austin Dailey, attorney for the applicant,40 SE 11th Avenue, summarized research on air curtain incinerator (ACI) emissions, noting that these devices recirculate and reburn emissions, significantly reducing pollutants compared to open burning. Primary outputs are CO\u8322?, water vapor, and minimal particulate matter (PM2.5), with visible smoke controlled to about 10% opacity under EPA standards. Studies from Oregon, Arizona, and the USDA show ACIs reduce PM2.5 emissions by over 80% and carbon monoxide by over 90% compared to traditional burning methods, while meeting national air quality standards. Ash and char byproducts can be repurposed for uses such as fertilizer. Mr. Dailey emphasized that ACIs offer a cleaner, environmentally friendly alternative for vegetative debris disposal and pose minimal impact on air quality beyond the immediate site.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer asked Mr. Roberts about the required setbacks in relation to the current debris pile at the landfill. Mr. Roberts explained that the proposed ordinance measures setbacks from the property boundary of the materials recovery facility, which is separate from the landfill parcel. He noted that the landfill scenario differs and referenced a recent fire in Dunnellon as an example of risks associated with large debris piles and chipping/grinding methods. Mr. Roberts emphasized that air curtain incinerators provide a safer, more controlled alternative for managing vegetative debris and offered to address public concerns later in the discussion.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 Tim Haines, Gray, Ackerman & Haines Law Firm, representing West Oak Developers, expressed opposition to the proposed ordinance, citing land use and safety concerns. He argued that air curtain incinerators are not appropriate adjacent to residential neighborhoods and that the ordinance lacks evidence of safety for urban settings. From a land use perspective, he stated that burning large amounts of material constitutes \ldblquote materials destruction,\rdblquote not recovery, and conflicts with existing code provisions requiring processing inside enclosed structures. He warned that allowing this as a use by right could enable placement on numerous industrial parcels citywide, rather than requiring site-specific review through a special use permit.\par
\par
Mr. Haines also noted that the Friends Recycling property was previously designated for future revitalization under the city\rquote s vision plan, and its proximity to a major residential redevelopment - including affordable housing - makes the proposed use incompatible. He raised environmental concerns, citing city policy discouraging burning due to greenhouse gas emissions, and asserted that air curtain incinerators produce more CO\u8322? than traditional burning. He further questioned the adequacy of testing, noting studies were limited to forest material and did not address heavy metals, chemicals, or PM10 particulates. Finally, he criticized reliance on opacity tests for compliance, stating they provide minimal safeguards.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 David Latham, Environmental Consultant (representing West Oak Developers), Geosyntec Consultants, Jacksonville, FL, opposed the ordinance, citing health and safety concerns. He noted that while air curtain incinerators reduce visible emissions, they still release PM2.5 particulates, which both EPA and FDEP recognize as harmful to human health. He emphasized that similar facilities typically operate on large, remote sites with substantial setbacks, unlike the proposed location near residential areas, some less than 600 feet away. Mr. Latham warned that incinerators can generate large volumes of ash, posing fire and respiratory hazards if mismanaged. He shared calculations estimating annual PM2.5 emissions equivalent to those from approximately 3,300 idling diesel trucks, highlighting long-term health risks such as reduced lung function and cardiovascular issues. He also stated that FDEP advised against locating such facilities in urban or suburban settings and concluded that the proposed use presents significant environmental and public health concerns.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 Jon Harvey, Tillman Associates & Engineering, 1720 SE 16th Avenue, Building 100, \tab Ocala, FL, recommended that air curtain incinerators be considered only through a special exception process rather than as a permitted use by right. He cautioned that allowing them outright in M2 or M3 zoning could enable placement near residential areas without public input. Mr. Harvey cited the city\rquote s comprehensive plan, which requires development to be compatible with neighboring uses, and noted that the proposed location is near homes, a hospital, and a church, making it inconsistent with the vision plan for the area as a gateway corridor. He also raised concerns about uncontrolled burning of landscaping materials that may contain pesticides or chemicals, stating the ordinance lacks safeguards to prevent harmful emissions.\par
\par
Scott Siemen, West Oak Developers, 2201 NW 21st Street, Ocala, FL, announced that the Madison Oaks East senior affordable housing project (102 units) has been approved by Florida Housing and is expected to begin construction by April. He thanked the council and staff for their support but expressed strong opposition to the proposed ordinance, stating that allowing air curtain incinerators near this development contradicts the city\rquote s goals for revitalization and affordable housing. He emphasized that seniors are highly vulnerable to respiratory issues and cited data linking PM2.5 exposure to significant health risks, including thousands of deaths annually. Mr. Siemen noted prior objections to landfill expansions and stated this proposal undermines the spirit of partnership between the city and West Oak Developers. He urged the council not to approve the ordinance or permit burn boxes within city limits.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 David Tillman, Tillman Associates & Engineering, 1720 SE 16th Avenue, Building 100, Ocala, FL, expressed strong opposition to placing an air curtain incinerator adjacent to or on top of a C&D landfill, citing severe fire risks. He warned that landfill fires are extremely difficult to extinguish and can smolder for years, referencing past incidents such as the Baseline Road stump dump fire. He argued that introducing a burn source where none currently exists represents a 100% increase in fire risk and emissions, not a reduction, and noted that loading debris into the incinerator disrupts the air curtain, causing smoke plumes throughout the day. Mr. Tillman emphasized that FDEP does not recommend locating such facilities in urban areas and highlighted the potential for significant particulate emissions (estimated at 37,000 pounds annually) impacting nearby neighborhoods. He urged the council to consider these safety and environmental hazards before approving the ordinance.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 Narvella Haynes, 2916 NW 3rd Terrace, Ocala, FL, spoke in support of Friends Recycling and its owner, noting his longstanding commitment to transparency, community engagement, and charitable contributions, including youth programs and annual school supply drives. She emphasized that the owner has consistently sought to build positive relationships and uphold safety and beautification promises. While acknowledging she is not an expert on the technical aspects, Ms. Haynes stated that if the proposed burn box is limited to clean wood, produces no pollution, and poses no health risks, opposition seems unnecessary. She expressed trust in city staff to ensure community safety.\tab Mr. Roberts shared a video demonstrating the difference between open burning and air curtain incineration, emphasizing the latter\rquote s ability to significantly reduce smoke and emissions. He addressed concerns raised during public comments, noting that air curtain incinerators have been permitted and operated in developed areas across Florida, including sites near residential properties, and provided examples with permit numbers. He argued that the proposed ordinance includes robust safeguards - such as setbacks, operational plans, and compliance with stringent state and federal standards - and asserted that the technology offers a cleaner, safer alternative to current disposal methods, which involve chipping and burying vegetative debris that generates methane, a more harmful greenhouse gas than CO\u8322?.\par
\par
Mr. Roberts stated that the proposed site is in a heavily industrialized area, with the nearest residential lot approximately 1,500 feet away, and that studies show negligible off-site impacts beyond 900 feet. He reiterated that approval would not grant automatic operation; the applicant would still need to meet all permitting and compliance requirements, and the council could require additional oversight through development agreements. He concluded that the ordinance provides a well-regulated, environmentally responsible option for managing vegetative debris and aligns with best practices adopted in other jurisdictions.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 Council Pro Tem Musleh asked for clarification on Mr. Robert\rquote s comments about \ldblquote no mothballing\rdblquote . Mr. Roberts explained there is no intention for the incinerators to sit dormant on the site; the intention is likely to be used on a weekly basis, condition permitting. . \par
\par
Council Member Mansfield asked for clarification on the proposed location of the incinerators. Mr. Roberts explained the location would be determined in the site plan, but that it would never be on top of the landfill. He further spoke to air quality concerns. The applicant must comply with FDEP standards; and the safety concern was addressed by the Fire Chief. The subject property will be required to have a fire suppression system. \par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
Fire Chief Clint Welborn stated that the fire department\rquote s initial concerns regarding setbacks and safety in the original draft of the ordinance have been addressed. He confirmed that the proposed incinerator would not be located on a landfill and reiterated that landfill fires are extremely difficult to extinguish and can burn for extended periods. Based on the revised ordinance and current plans, the fire department has no remaining safety concerns.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440\par
Fire Marshall Clayton Anderson explained the daily burn permit regulations established by the Florida Forestry Service. He advised City Council that permit issuance is based on weather conditions. Furthermore, he confirmed an inspection is performed before a burn permit is issued. \par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 Council Member Musleh expressed concern regarding changing weather conditions. \par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 President Bethea thanked all parties for their input and emphasized the need to balance innovative solutions for debris management with community health and safety. He acknowledged the concerns raised by residents and experts and stressed that any approved approach must include strong safeguards, oversight, and compliance measures to protect nearby neighborhoods.\tab Mr. Roberts noted that various types of incinerators, including air curtain units, are already used throughout Ocala under state permitting, which the city cannot preempt. He emphasized that the proposed ordinance introduces stricter standards and oversight compared to current practices. Roberts provided examples of permitted air curtain incinerators operating near residential areas, schools, churches, and even airports in Florida, asserting that the technology is well-established and widely accepted. He stated that larger incinerator boxes are more effective and safer than smaller, portable units due to better air curtain performance.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1 Mr. Roberts argued that the ordinance brings transparency and robust regulation to a process that currently occurs with less oversight, ensuring clear rules and safeguards. He added that while cost savings are not the primary consideration, this method is significantly less expensive than current disposal practices and offers a practical, environmentally responsible alternative for managing vegetative debris as the city grows.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty expressed concern that the ordinance appears tailored to accommodate a specific site, noting the ten-acre requirement and potential for other facilities, such as Waste Pro, to qualify with minimal expansion. He questioned whether this could lead to multiple incinerators in the same area, raising community concerns about emissions regardless of technical assurances. Hilty also highlighted inconsistencies regarding truck traffic, pointing out that previous objections to increased traffic near the landfill are now being reversed to justify the proposal. He suggested the ordinance may create economic advantages for the applicant but could introduce broader impacts on infrastructure and neighborhoods.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440\par
Mr. Roberts noted Friends Recycling currently disposes of vegetative material. \par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 Council Member Dreyer stated she would vote \ldblquote no\rdblquote on the ordinance as written, citing quality-of-life concerns for nearby residents. She suggested that if the council supports the concept, changes should include limiting the use to C&D landfills rather than materials recovery facilities and requiring approval through a special exception permit rather than as a use by right. Ms. Dreyer emphasized that the proposed location does not make sense given its proximity to residential development and raised equity concerns, noting that historically undesirable uses have been placed in minority neighborhoods. She concluded that the ordinance introduces too many unknowns regarding pollution, smoke, and truck traffic and does not align with community values.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sl276\slmult1\tx1440 There being no further discussion the motion to adopt the ordinance failed by roll call vote.\par
\pard\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\sl252\slmult1\cf1\kerning2\f0\fs24 City Manager Pete Lee opened the workshop by noting that the Vision 2050 draft is a long-awaited update and an important step forward for the City. He explained that Vision 2050 serves as a recalibration of the previous Vision 2035 plan, which has been a critical tool in guiding priorities and implementing strategies over the years. Mr. Lee emphasized that the new vision will help maintain the community\rquote s desired character and set a blueprint for future growth.\par
\par
Growth Management Director Jeff Shrum then provided a brief overview of the draft Vision 2050 plan. He introduced Planning Director Audrey Hill and consultant Ali Palmer from Kimley-Horn & Associates, who assisted in developing the plan. Mr. Shrum encouraged Council members to consider what their vision for 2050 looks like, posing questions about future development patterns, population and demographic changes, governance challenges, and transportation innovations. He stressed that while predicting 25 years ahead is difficult, the vision document provides essential guidance for shaping the City\rquote s future. Mr. Shrum concluded by turning the presentation over to planning staff for a detailed review of the draft Vision 2050.\par
\par
Planning Director Aubrey Hale introduced the structure and purpose of the Vision 2050 document, explaining that it is divided into six sections, with the first five forming the core of the plan. These sections include the story of the vision, citywide initiatives, focus areas, and key next steps for implementation. Mr. Hale noted that Vision 2050 builds upon Vision 2035, refining its principles and continuing its emphasis on economic diversification, vibrant neighborhoods, and a strong urban center.\par
\par
He explained that the document identifies high-priority initiatives to be achieved within the next five years, followed by future considerations for six to ten years. Vision 2050 also introduces urban form opportunities, which focus on creating higher-density, mixed-use areas through context-driven, form-based codes rather than traditional zoning. State Road 40 was highlighted as a major corridor for connectivity and development.\par
\par
Mr. Hale emphasized the community engagement process, noting that over 1,000 participants contributed input through outreach and focus groups. He also reviewed accomplishments from Vision 2035, including the consolidation of land use categories, adoption of form-based codes for downtown and midtown, and major updates to the comprehensive plan.\par
\par
He concluded by stressing that Vision 2050 is a dynamic document that will require periodic updates. To support public access, he introduced a QR code that links to the plan and related resources.\par
\par
Chief Planning Official Endira Madraveren focused on Section 2 of the Vision 2050 document, which addresses bringing the vision to life. She noted that many long-term goals from Vision 2035 have been accomplished and will continue to guide the City\rquote s future. Ms. Madraveren emphasized leveraging Community Redevelopment Agency funding before its sunset for projects such as the redevelopment of North Magnolia and streetscape improvements along major corridors. She also highlighted ongoing efforts to activate West Ocala through redevelopment of brownfield sites, including the Mary Sue Rich Community Center at Reed Place.\par
\par
Ms. Madraveren described the extensive community engagement process, which included four citywide summits and 23 outreach sessions with strategic groups and departments. This input helped build consensus and shape the long-term implementation of Vision 2050.\par
\par
Mr. Hale then discussed the role of consultants in the process, including Kimley-Horn and Urban3. Urban3 provided an analysis of land value economics and evidence-based design, revealing key insights such as the higher return on investment from mixed-use development compared to large single-use properties. Their findings showed that downtown mixed-use blocks generate significantly more value per acre than big-box retail sites, reinforcing the importance of infill development.\par
\par
Mr. Hale also reviewed trends and projections, noting that Ocala\rquote s population is expected to grow by nearly 31 percent by 2050, reaching approximately 92,000 residents. He explained that Vision 2050 introduces four building blocks to guide growth: land use and housing, mobility and connectivity, public and open spaces, and gateways. These components will shape citywide initiatives, focus areas, and opportunities for catalytic development and redevelopment.\par
\par
Mr. Hale explained that the Ocala 2050 plan updates the earlier 2035 vision, keeping many of the same elements like complete streets, trails, land use, and the heat map. The major new feature is \ldblquote urban form opportunities\rdblquote marked by blue dots - areas where the city can encourage denser development to increase tax revenue. He then highlighted key action items, including updating the land development code, maintaining the capital improvement program, incentivizing infill development, refining special districts, using CRA tools for redevelopment, supporting workforce training, and evaluating annexation through ROI analysis. He also covered mobility priorities such as mobility fees, transportation project planning, expanding transit, supporting Rails-to-Trails, and improving pedestrian safety and complete streets.\par
\par
Ms. Madraveren outlined actions for recreation, cultural spaces, gateways, and focus areas in the Ocala 2050 plan. She highlighted updating the parks master plan to assess park needs, identifying sites for new regional sports complexes, and creating a master plan for further improvements at Tuscawilla Park. She described integrating open-space requirements into the development code and using mapping to guide future public art installations. She then covered gateway enhancements - developing a citywide plan, setting design standards, and improving key corridors like SR 40 and I-75. Finally, she reviewed four focus areas (East Ocala, Central Core, West Ocala, Airport), noting planned mixed-use development, catalytic sites, regional park opportunities, and trail connections, with emphasis on SR 40 as a major east-west corridor.\par
\par
Mr. Hale reviewed the final focus areas in the Ocala 2050 vision. For the High-Intensity Central Core, he noted that earlier catalytic sites have already developed, so new potential redevelopment areas - especially Midtown, underused parking lots, and areas around Tuscawilla Park - are now being identified. He emphasized strengthening connections along SR 40, extending complete streets into the hospital district, and updating older studies and the Tuscawilla master plan.\par
\par
In the West Ocala Focus Area, he highlighted MLK Avenue as the spine, with key catalytic intersections along SR 40 and US 27. Priorities include expanding the Heritage Trail, attracting essential industries like a grocery store, streamlining approvals, and using the CRA to support redevelopment.\par
\par
For the Airport Focus Area, he described its industrial character, the need to activate city-owned airport industrial park property, improved roadway connections, and a strong community request for expanding SunTran fixed-route service to the airport.\par
\par
He closed by outlining next steps: adopting the 2050 vision, amending the comprehensive plan, updating the outdated land-development code, aligning regulations with the new vision, and refreshing older master plans so they reflect current conditions and future goals.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh asked for clearer data on total city green space, noting that the public often confuses vacant land with parks, DRAs, and other open spaces. Mr. Hale said the 11% figure reflects only undeveloped land and does not include parks or DRAs. City Manager Lee added staff can calculate total green-space acreage and provide clearer reporting, which will be refined through the upcoming Recreation and Parks Master Plan update.\par
\par
Mr. Lee emphasized that the vision is a guiding - not regulatory - document that helps prioritize the city\rquote s work program. He highlighted the importance of downtown, West Ocala, SR 40, the airport, and parks, and stressed aligning growth and redevelopment strategies with the Urban3 study, maintenance obligations, transportation planning, and careful annexation decisions. He added that refining permitting and inspection systems is essential for efficiency, and overall, the vision provides the tool needed to organize and advance these ambitious priorities.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield asked how the City can encourage redevelopment of privately owned downtown industrial properties. Mr. Lee explained that the updated vision identifies broader catalytic areas and that the City now has more tools, such as CRA programs and brownfield incentives, to help transition underused industrial sites. He said the City often works directly with property owners or through public-private partnerships to support redevelopment, noting similar approaches used for recent downtown projects.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer noted that the School Board is preparing to sell nearby surplus properties and encouraged the City to engage early so the sites can be redeveloped in ways that maximize value for the School Board and align with the City\rquote s vision.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer asked whether initiatives from the TDC\rquote s GAP Study were incorporated into the 2050 vision. Staff explained that while the study came in late and was not directly included, they were mindful of it during planning and can review it again to integrate any structurally compatible ideas. Mr. Hale added that some urban-form opportunity areas were influenced by earlier conversations related to the GAP Study, particularly in the southwest.\par
\par
Mayor Maricano asked how the 2050 Vision should guide annual City priorities. Mr. Lee explained that the vision functions as a toolbox: some initiatives are ongoing, while others will shift in priority as projects are completed and community needs evolve. He noted that tools like the CRA, form-based codes, and corridor plans will continue to guide work, and priorities may change year to year. Mr. Shrum added that the Transportation Improvement Program and the Capital Improvement Program provide the annual mechanism to align capital projects with the long-term vision.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer asked whether any single city serves as a model for the 2050 Vision. Mr. Lee responded that no single place fits perfectly, but several cities offer useful components or best practices, such as Greenville (SC), Panama City, Huntsville, Winter Park, and Winter Garden. He emphasized that Ocala must adapt ideas to its own character, noting strong \ldblquote bones\rdblquote for continued downtown growth. He highlighted ongoing needs such as connectivity improvements across SR 40, enhanced walkability, and increasing downtown residents, workers, and visitors to support a more vibrant, 16-hour-a-day downtown.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh praised the inclusion of both the airport and east-side areas in the vision, noting the airport district\rquote s long-untapped potential and urging continued focus on activating the airport industrial park. Mr. Shrum said the vision is designed to align with the airport\rquote s master plan and future passenger-service opportunities. Council President Bethea commented that recent West Ocala investments, such as West Oak, Water Recharge Park, and the Mary Sue Rich Center, show how vision work becomes tangible progress, and emphasized continuing efforts on connectivity, housing, and redevelopment in that area. Council Members noted that Ocala has drawn from other cities\rquote successful ideas and that this draft provides a strong foundation for moving into the 2050 planning phase.\par
\par
Mr. Hale encouraged Council members to review the draft vision document, send any edits or suggestions within the next few weeks, and noted staff is preparing to bring a final version forward soon. Mr. Shrum added that the Planning Commission had just reviewed the draft and that public hearings are expected around April or May, with public feedback available through the posted QR code. Mr. Lee noted a few inaccuracies still need to be cleaned up before wider release. Council President Bethea requested a media effort to notify the public about the QR code and feedback opportunity, and staff agreed.\par
\pard\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Council Member Musleh expressed concern about the monies coming from carry-forward from previous years' budgets, especially if they are coming from accounts unrelated to building expenses.\par
\par
Police Chief Mike Balken confirmed the carry-forward monies in the budget will be allocated towards the project cost. He will provide a list of the carryforward items from prior years to Council Member Musleh. Chief Balken confirmed the buildout will take approximately four to six months. \par
\par
Council Member Musleh informed City Manager Pete Lee the carry-forward concerns need to be addressed. He suggested big projects be put into reserve funds rather than carry-forward. He also informed Chief Balken his comments are not directed at this item specifically, but rather the bigger picture. Mr. Lee confirmed the City is evaluating the use of carry-forward monies as staff prepares the budget. \par
\par
Council Member Hilty discussed how the carry-forward option allows unspent, unobligated funds from one fiscal year to move into the next, preventing the loss of budgeted money and enhancing fiscal efficiency.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer suggested allocating carry-forward (or carryover) funds from the City\rquote s operating budget to a reserve fund to maintain financial stability.\par
\par
Mr. Lee discussed the changed staff is making in budgeting and auditing practices. \par
\par
Council Member Musleh explained how allocating carry-forward money, unspent funds from a previous budget period moved to a new one, is generally considered not helpful for determining which specific projects saved money, because it obscures the true performance of the current budget cycle.\par
\par
There being no further discussion the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\f1\par

The proposed rezoning is consistent with the existing Employment Center Future Land Use classification and pursuant to Section 122-244 of the Code of Ordinances. \par
\par
To note, the Planning & Zoning Commission and staff recommend approval. Furthermore, she confirmed the applicant is working on vacating existing tenants from the property with Council President Bethea. \par
\par
Rodney Rogers, Applicant\rquote s Attorney, 1105 SE 3\super rd\nosupersub Avenue, discussed progress made by the applicant on the subject properties: one building was demolished and the second building is undergoing abatement. To note, the property owner has a sale pending for the frontage portion of the property, and they plan to sell the remainder of the properties under the proposed rezoning to support the surrounding industrial uses.\par
\par
No public comment.\par
\par
There being no further discussion the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Jim Mikula, Rosewood Homeowners Association President, 3624 SE 18th Avenue, addressed the City Council to report ongoing property damage and safety concerns caused by fiber installation vendors. He highlighted a recent gas line rupture that required an emergency response from Ocala Fire Rescue, as well as numerous instances of damaged lawns, exposed cables, and abandoned lines left by unidentified crews. Mr. Mikula noted that these vendors consistently fail to provide advance notice or identification to residents, leaving the community without a clear point of contact for complaints. On behalf of the HOA, he expressed a strong desire to partner with the City to advocate for policy changes that would increase vendor liability and mandate stricter requirements for site restoration and resident notification at all levels of government.\par
\par
City Manager, Pete Lee\f1\fs22 \f0\fs24 clarified that while fiber installation vendors must obtain permits and notify the Engineering Department of their projects, the City is not provided with specific start or end dates. He emphasized that vendors are prohibited from entering private property without homeowner consent and noted that the City may seek legislative changes to address these issues.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh expressed deep frustration regarding the negative impact these vendors have had on local residents. \par
\par
Mr. Lee stated that it is unacceptable for fiber installation vendors to cause gas leaks, damage residential lawns, or leave cables exposed.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty inquired whether the City could mandate that vendors inform Homeowners Associations (HOAs) prior to beginning a project. City Attorney William Sexton explained that current statutes prohibit the City from requiring vendors to notify residents or HOAs of their planned projects.\par
\par
Council President Bethea requested that the City contact state departments to explain these ongoing issues and seek formal assistance. Mr. Lee confirmed that the City will reach out to both State and Federal offices for support.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield reported receiving numerous public complaints regarding fiber vendors, including an incident where a vendor struck a gas line and disrupted local business operations. He voiced support for multi-level government intervention and suggested the City explore developing its own cable infrastructure as a long-term solution.\par
Mr. Lee stated the City will conduct research to determine the total time and financial resources spent addressing disruptions like electrical outages and gas leaks, noting that vendors are responsible for the costs of any damages they cause.\par
\par
Fire Chief Clint Welborn reported that the department has been documenting the manpower and time required to respond to vendor-related incidents for several months and will provide a detailed report on the costs associated with gas leak responses.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield expressed concern regarding the significant City time and funding currently being spent to rectify problems caused by these vendors.\par
\par
Council President Bethea informed Mr. Mikula that the City will engage with State and Federal government officials to address these concerns.\par
\par
Assistant City Manager, Ken Whitehead, stated that vendors are required to obtain a right-of-way permit and post a $500,000 bond.\par
\par
City Engineer Sean Lanier noted that most vendors have filed these bonds with the City, which remain active until a project is completed. He explained that the City can file claims against these bonds on behalf of impacted residents.\par
\par
Mr. Whitehead advised that the City is assisting homeowners with property damage by directing them to file claims through the City, which then coordinates with vendors to ensure repairs are funded.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer requested that the City work directly with the Rosewood Homeowners Association residents to facilitate their damage claims.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield urged the City to take a proactive stance in advocating for governmental changes to protect the public.\par
\par
Mr. Lee informed Council Member Dreyer that these vendor projects are typically completed within a few days.\par
\par
Director of Electric Utility, Doug Peebles, advised Council Member Mansfield that utility "locates" are only valid for 30 days and noted that underground installation is necessary because the City\rquote s utility poles are currently at capacity.\par
\par
Mr. Lee stated that this matter has been added to the City\rquote s Legislative Priorities List for the year and that a draft letter will be provided for City Council review tomorrow.\par
\par
Mr. Sexton reported that the City has already sued one vendor to recover $110,000 in damages for a sewer line break and suggested partnering with other affected municipalities to lobby state and federal officials for relief.\par
\f2\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Levonda Goodson, CEO, provided an overview of services and recent progress at the Estella Byrd Whitman Wellness and Community Resource Center. She highlighted that the center offers comprehensive primary care for all ages, chronic disease management, telehealth visits, in\u8209?house lab work, medication dispensing at low cost, and patient transportation to appointments and specialists.\par
\par
Ms. Goodson reported significant growth in patient visits:\par
\bullet 2023 - 321 visits\par
\bullet 2024 - nearly 3,000 visits (749 unduplicated patients)\par
\bullet 2025 - nearly 4,000 visits (811 unduplicated patients)\par
\par
She emphasized the importance of community partnerships with SMA, the Marion County Hospital District, Community Home Project, Marion Senior Services, Interfaith Emergency Services, the Community Paramedicine Program, and CareWise Pharmacy.\par
\par
Ms. Goodson noted ongoing funding needs common to nonprofits and encouraged continued partnerships, advocacy, and community awareness to support expanded access to primary care. She stated the center now operates two locations and remains committed to providing a medical home that reduces emergency room use and strengthens community stability.\par
\par
City Manager Pete Lee commended Ms. Goodson and her team for their dedicated service and unwavering support of underserved communities.\par
\f1\par

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\froman\fprq2\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 City Manager Pete Lee presented a draft letter addressed to the Florida Legislature regarding fiber installation contractor complaints and regulatory remedies, requesting Council feedback before finalization.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh inquired about the status of $2.8 million in damages caused by fiber contractors; Chief of Staff Christopher Watt responded that while specific totals are pending from the PMA broker, 12 recent gas leak claims exceeded $8,000, and he committed to adding the exact unreimbursed damage amount to the draft letter.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh emphasized the critical need to quantify unreimbursed damages, leading Mr. Watt to confirm he would work with the City\rquote s broker to determine that figure for inclusion in the legislative letter.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh raised serious public safety concerns regarding damaged gas and sewer lines, questioning why contractors continue to make catastrophic mistakes that jeopardize lives and property.\par
\par
Council Member Manfield highlighted that fiber contractors are draining City resources through unreimbursed utility locates and property damages.\par
\par
Director of Electric Utility Doug Peebles reported that while the exact financial impact is difficult to determine, the high volume of utility locate requests is severely burdening department operations.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer recommended strengthening the letter\rquote s tone to be more aggressive, suggesting it include a detailed list of anecdotal and physical evidence regarding damages to both public and private property.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield reiterated that the letter must address the broader financial burden placed on City resources beyond direct physical damages.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh noted that residents are "terrified" of fiber contractors due to past safety incidents and stressed the importance of tracking damage costs, reimbursement status, and the frequency of repeat call-outs to the same locations.\par
\par
Director Peebles acknowledged the data limitations of current City systems but confirmed that the department is working to address the ongoing issue of frequent contractor call-outs.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh questioned why some contractors had not posted the required $500,000 bond; Mr. Lee confirmed all but one contractor, Wire3, were bonded and admitted it was a City error to allow that firm to begin work without one.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh proposed increasing the bond requirement to $1 million for fiber contractors and noted he would personally meet with a new contractor next week to discuss public safety expectations.\par
\par
Mr. Lee explained that while federal grants are driving these projects, the City\rquote s regulatory authority is limited by federal law; however, the City will implement a new tracking system for locates, costs, bonds, and damages.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer requested that the letter include requirements for visible business signage on contractor vehicles and improved public notification protocols, such as City-issued door hangers for upcoming projects.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield suggested that the costs associated with hanging door hangers and other administrative hours should be billed directly to the fiber companies.\par
\par
City Attorney Sexton clarified that while Florida statutes restrict local control over fiber contractors, the City maintains the right to claim all incurred costs, though quantifying "neighborhood terror" or pain and suffering remains a legal challenge.\par
\par
Mr. Watt confirmed the City tracks claims until they are paid by insurance carriers and promised to provide the Council with a comprehensive list of all paid and pending claims.\par
\par
City Attorney Sexton discussed a previous litigation case where the City settled a $197,000 claim for $110,000, highlighting the difficulty in proving specific damages like pavement resurfacing frequency.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer recommended that the draft letter include specific legislative recommendations to amend the Florida statutes that currently limit the City\rquote s oversight.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh expressed disappointment that the State Legislature has yet to address the safety and financial concerns of Ocala citizens regarding fiber installation.\par
\par
Mr. Lee concluded by stating the City would follow up with the Council via email to provide all available financial data and updates.\par
\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 City Manager Pete Lee reported that Florida House Bill 399 (HB 399) is scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027, pending any legal challenges, and identified seven key areas that will directly impact municipal land use and development regulations. Regarding development permits and orders, Mr. Lee explained that the City must conduct a fee study to ensure charges are reasonably related to direct processing costs; he advised Council Member Musleh that this study could be performed by internal staff rather than a third party. The City is currently collaborating with the Technical Working Group (TWG) on the School Interlocal Agreement as part of the broader regulatory response to the bill. Mr. Lee noted that residential compatibility reviews will necessitate amendments to the Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Regulations to include specific definitions for compatible, incompatible, and complementary land uses. Current regulations governing residential manufactured homes will become unenforceable under the new law, requiring the City to execute comprehensive changes to ensure local codes remain consistent with state mandates. Staff is conducting further research into Section 7 of HB 399, which limits the regulation of buildings constructed offsite as defined by Florida Statute 553.36 and introduces new language regarding architectural elements.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer expressed strong opposition to the bill, characterizing it as state-level micromanagement and oversight that threatens local zoning integrity by suggesting that "not everything belongs everywhere."\f1\fs22 \f0\fs24 In response to concerns about mobile homes being placed in inappropriate areas, Council Member Dreyer stated she would call for a building moratorium to protect the City\rquote s wooded fields and rural character.\par
\par
Mr. Lee assured the Council that staff will perform an in-depth analysis of all sections of the statute to determine where the City retains the authority to govern the exterior aesthetics and placement of mobile homes.\f1\fs22 \f0\fs24 He cautioned that the implementation of the bill has the potential to significantly alter the established character of the Ocala community.\par
\par
Council Member Musleh observed that the sweeping changes in the bill will have a visible impact on every quadrant of the City.\par
\par
Mr. Lee raised concerns regarding the "Live Local" language as it relates to manufactured homes, noting that while it is considered an affordable housing product, its specific application within the City remains a point of inquiry.\par
\par
Director of Community Development Services, James Haynes, discussed provisions allowing religious institutions to develop affordable housing on sites of three acres or more under the Live Local Act.\par
\f2\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 City Manager Pete Lee introduced the topic by asking City Engineer Sean Lanier to explain the roadway project and why its design now needed updates. Mr. Lanier explained that the design was completed and approved in 2022, but FDOT is now requesting the project documents be updated to meet current standards. \par
\par
Council Pro Tem Musleh questioned how the project expanded from one roundabout to four within roughly a mile of roadway, saying it seemed excessive even with federal funding. Council Member Hilty added concerns about the fire station and police substation located mid\u8209?corridor and questioned whether emergency vehicles could safely navigate multiple roundabouts.\par
\par
Mr. Lanier responded that the final design had been reviewed with the Fire Department, and all turning and access requirements were met. He then explained the purpose behind the roundabouts: reducing speeding and crashes, eliminating the need for traffic signal maintenance, and preventing drivers from \ldblquote racing the light\rdblquote as they currently do on Third Street. He also explained that two roundabouts serve existing intersections, while a third would serve a future park entrance, and the fourth is at Ninth Street, where traffic volume justifies the design. He added that the design aligns with the planned streetscape improvements and helps calm traffic on a road that is currently too wide.\par
\par
Council President Bethea emphasized that four roundabouts in such a short distance felt like over\u8209?engineering. Council Member Dreyer noted the fire station is located in the middle of the four proposed roundabouts, so they wouldn't be traveling through all four. She further noted that residents in the northern section struggle to make left turns because of heavy traffic and has been asked by residents whether a traffic light had been considered, and called it a "no brainer" to calm traffic and increase pedestrian and resident safety. Mr. Lee agreed, pointing out the long, uninterrupted stretch between intersections, saying this contributes to dangerous speeding.\par
\par
Mr. Lee responded that the project originated in the Midtown Plan, designed to improve cross\u8209?connectivity between east and west neighborhoods and support ongoing CRA investments in housing and historic rehabilitation. They stressed that pedestrians currently do not feel safe crossing the road, and roundabouts would break up speed, shorten crossing distances, and provide natural \ldblquote checkpoints\rdblquote for traffic.\par
\par
At the end of discussion, Council Member Dreyer suggested staff include proposed designs in future similar prsentations to allow Council to visualize the concepts. Mr. Lee agreed and clariried that the vote before Council was only to approve necessary design updates to satisfy federal requirements for the project\rquote s 2027 funding. \par
\par
The Council then moved the item forward with the understanding that staff will refine the layout and return with a recommended final design.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Planning Director Aubrey Hale explained a series of interconnected requests related to a large mixed\u8209?use project, beginning with the removal of outdated comprehensive plan policies that only affected portions of the property. He noted that the state had no objections to dropping these policies, aside from FDOT\rquote s reminder to continue coordinating on traffic impacts as development proceeds. Mr. Hale outlined how the applicant is replacing old policy constraints with a new planned development (PD), which will establish current standards for land use, density, and buffering. He walked through the PD\rquote s \ldblquote bubble plan,\rdblquote showing where commercial, mixed\u8209?use, multifamily, and single\u8209?family areas would be located, and detailing maximum dwelling counts, commercial square footage, building\u8209?height limits, and required buffers, especially along existing neighborhoods. Staff recommended approval with conditions, including lighting, service provision, easements, adherence to B\u8209?2 standards, density controls, and enhanced perimeter landscaping.\par
\par
Attorney Fred Roberts, speaking for the applicant, emphasized that the complex set of agenda items reflects decades of legacy agreements and outdated policies tied to earlier development rules. The 19\u8209?month application process, he explained, was necessary to modernize those requirements and replace them with a single, clear PD framework. Mr. Roberts noted that the applicant met with neighbors early on and made several changes in response: adjusting product types along the edges, expanding buffers, adding an opaque fence, restricting certain uses, and limiting density to levels consistent with low\u8209?intensity standards even though the site qualifies for higher. He described the project as a long\u8209?term, mixed\u8209?use development intended to transition well with surrounding neighborhoods and serve as a legacy project for the area.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty expressed concern that continued development could depress existing homeowners\rquote property values, especially for residents who bought at high prices but hold low interest rates and now feel financially trapped. He warned that falling home values could shrink the tax base and harm constituents, and he argued that the city may need to pause growth to protect current residents and address school overcrowding.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer responded with local market data, explaining that while some county areas outside the city are experiencing price softening due to new construction, the City of Ocala itself is not seeing price declines and remains in high demand. She noted that most listings are outside city limits and that within the city, sales remain strong, inventory is limited, and many units are pre\u8209?sold. She clarified that the project under discussion was already approved years ago and is simply being updated to modern zoning standards, not increasing density beyond what is allowed. Council Member Dreyer emphasized that the city has required infrastructure to be completed before development in past cases and that public frustrations often stem from misunderstanding how the process works. Council Member Hilty concluded by saying he appreciated hearing the issue from her financial perspective.\par
\par
Council Pro Tem Musleh noted regardless of Council's vote tonight, the applicant could move forward with pulling permits and start building; the project has already been approved. He stated he thinks it is a well thought out project, and noted that the property was never planned to be a wildlife refuge.\par
\par
There being no further discussion the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Chip Griffin addressed Council regarding concerns about the City continuing to operate and invest in Ocala Fiber while competing with private internet providers. He cited multiple personal and business experiences involving delayed installations, billing issues, higher pricing, contract requirements, and slower response times compared to private competitors, which he stated were offering faster service at lower costs with quicker installation and repair times. Mr. Griffin questioned the justification for additional City investment in Ocala Fiber given the increasing number of private providers available and expressed concern that the network was unable to compete effectively in the current market.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty acknowledged concerns regarding Ocala Fiber\rquote s competitiveness and stated that while the City must continue maintaining infrastructure to avoid outages for existing customers, private providers were increasingly offering lower-priced internet service and expanding aggressively throughout the community. He noted that Council had previously considered expanding the network through a bond issue but had not moved forward, and stated that a broader discussion was needed regarding the future direction of Ocala Fiber, particularly as the City appeared to be falling behind competitors.\par
\par
City Manager Pete Lee agreed with the concerns raised and stated that staff would schedule a workshop for Council to further discuss the issue and the future of the City\rquote s fiber network.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield expressed continued support for Ocala Fiber but stated the utility was not currently performing competitively in the open internet market. He raised concerns about continued financial investment in the system without a clear long-term strategy, noting increasing competition from numerous private providers and emphasizing that Ocala Fiber could not be treated like a traditional utility monopoly. Mr. Mansfield stated that the City needed to become more aggressive and responsive to market conditions, and suggested the possibility of outside assistance through consultants or public-private partnerships to improve operations and competitiveness. He emphasized the importance of providing high-quality fiber service to residents while ensuring the City does not continue investing funds without a realistic opportunity for return on investment.\par
\par
Council Pro Tem Musleh concurred with Council Member Mansfield's comments, noting this agenda item relates to necessary inventory purchases to keep the existing system functioning.\par
\par
City Manager Pete Lee explained that Ocala Fiber operates as an enterprise fund separate from the City\rquote s general fund and stated that the utility was still addressing longstanding systemic and infrastructure issues identified during earlier studies. Mr. Lee noted that the competitive landscape had changed significantly with the arrival of additional private providers, while the City continued working through procurement, design, and installation processes that move more slowly than those in the private sector. He stated the City\rquote s current plan focuses on incremental neighborhood expansion, improving backbone infrastructure, and evaluating opportunities for operational improvements and potential public-private partnerships. Mr. Lee also acknowledged customer concerns regarding pricing, installation timelines, and service performance, while emphasizing that the utility remains financially viable and continues to gain and retain customers.\par
\par
Chief Financial Officer Janice Mitchell stated the City has delayed issuing bonds for major expansion projects in order to ensure infrastructure planning and deployment strategies are fully prepared before borrowing funds. Ms. Mitchell explained that the City currently serves approximately 25 neighborhoods and plans to begin targeted promotional efforts in underutilized service areas, including marketing campaigns and promotional pricing intended to compete with private providers.\par
\par
Mr. Lee agreed to schedule a workshop for Council to review the results from Uptown's report, or sooner if the results are delayed.\par
\par
There being no further discussion the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Chief Planning Official Endira Madraveren presented a request to amend the Kenward at Heathbrook (formerly Keys at Ocala 2) PD, established in 2022. The amendment would change building types from duplexes to quadruplexes, allowing up to 146 units without increasing overall density, and reduce minimum lot width to 15 feet to allow fee\u8209?simple lots. Additional changes include revised internal layout and circulation, modified access with two points on Tartan Road and removal of access to SW 66th Street, and an increase in preserved open space from 41% to 53%. Staff found the amendment consistent with the existing PD, the Heathbrook DRI, and City code, with available utilities and no service issues identified. The Planning & Zoning Commission recommended denial due to proposed wetland reconfiguration, but staff maintains its recommendation of approval, noting minor clerical revisions since the P&Z review.\par
\par
Thomas Burkhart, 6580 SW 51st Court, expressed concerns about traffic impacts from removing access to SW 66th Street, noting that directing all traffic to Tartan Road would create congestion and that SW 66th is better suited to handle the volume. He also urged conservation of wetlands, citing significant wildlife activity in the area, and objected to replacing cul\u8209?de\u8209?sacs with dead ends, stating it would detract from the established Heathbrook aesthetic.\par
\par
Brian Hayes, 6560 SW 51st Court, presented visual materials comparing the currently approved plan with the proposed amendment. He stated that the existing plan better protects the wetlands and argued that building over wetland areas sacrifices a valuable natural resource without clear benefit to the City. He encouraged the Council to uphold the Planning and Zoning Commission\rquote s recommendation for denial and emphasized the importance of preserving environmental features.\par
\par
Kelly Haynes, 6560 SW 51st Court, addressed the Council and affirmed the concerns raised by previous speakers. She highlighted the Planning and Zoning Commission\rquote s April 13 recommendation for denial due to wetland destruction and urged the Council to consider that an approved plan already exists that preserves major wetland areas. She expressed appreciation for the City\rquote s long\u8209?term vision but asked that environmental impacts be given significant weight.\par
\par
Rob Batsel, 1531 SE 36 Ave, speaking on behalf of Eisenhower Property Group, presented an updated plan for the 32\u8209?acre site previously approved as the Keys at Ocala II. The revised proposal maintains the same 146 units but replaces the former apartment layout with a townhome product featuring garages, driveways, fewer buildings, and substantially increased open space (from 41% to 53%). Mr. Batsel noted that the plan has been approved by the Heath Brook Architectural Committee and includes enhanced landscaping and buffering along the east boundary. Access remains on Tartan Road with an emergency\u8209?only secondary access. Two deviations are requested relating to block lengths and reducing berm width to 10 feet, which the applicant stated still meets safety needs. Regarding wetlands, Mr. Batsel acknowledged a 1.6\u8209?acre impact but emphasized that the highest\u8209?value wetlands are preserved and that the design improves drainage performance. The project is undergoing state\u8209?level environmental and stormwater review, including a formal wetland delineation and review by the Southwest Florida Water Management District. \par
\par
Beau Clymer, Clymer Farner Barley, 2100 SE 17th St, Suite 202, explained that site grading, stormwater flows, and hydrology have been analyzed and meet regulatory requirements. Mr. Batsel concluded that the revised plan yields a better overall design with more open space, improved drainage, and minimized wetland impacts.\par
\par
With no further discussion, the motion carried by role call vote.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Chief Planning Official Endira Madraveren explained that the applicant is requesting an amendment to the Saving Mercy Planned Development to increase total residential units from 144 to 200, consisting of 20 duplexes and 180 multifamily units. The amendment also proposes raising the maximum building height from 35 to 45 feet, revising the development layout into four phases, and incorporating minor nonsubstantial updates. Staff noted that the 9.31\u8209?acre site is already developed with duplex units, an administrative office, and multifamily units under construction. The proposed density remains within the Employment Center Future Land Use maximum of 24 units per acre, and no new code variations are requested. Staff found the amendment consistent with the comprehensive plan and PD standards, confirmed utilities are available, and reported no level\u8209?of\u8209?service issues. The Planning and Zoning Commission recommended approval, and staff also recommended approval with conditions.\par
\par
Chuck Pigeon, Adore Group Inc. Engineering, stated he was available to answer questions and noted that phase two has experienced construction delays due to material supply issues. He also explained that increasing the height to 45 feet would allow a smaller building footprint, more open space, and better site design; although three stories may be partially visible, the building would be set farther from Silver Springs Boulevard.\par
\par
Mayor Marciano spoke about the high quality product being built and expressed his excitement for the affordable housing project. Council Member Dreyer agreed with the Mayor's comments.\par
\par
There being no furthr discussion the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Chief Planning Official Endira Madraveren discussed items 9b and 9c, a request for an expansion on a liquor license for the local business, Tipsy Skipper and Mutiny Bar, to allow for outdoor consumption within a designated sidewalk cafe.\par
\par
Sam Beatty, General Manager of Mutiny, explained his staff will enforce alcohol remaining within the cafe space by posting a door person to watch patrons and ensure they remain in the covered seating area with any alcohol.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer questioned whether police officers are checking people on the streets.\par
\par
Chief Balken discussed police concerns about outdoor drinking and questioned whether an establishment will always maintain a door person.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer noted there may be some general public confusion about public drinking, as other municipalities allow for moving around a designated area with open containers. She further noted she frequents the downtown late at night, as it is her district, to check what is happening. She commented both the Tipsy Skipper and Mutiny Bar provide a unique atmosphere for a clientele not otherwise catered to, and they currently have staff posted at the door to card everyone who patronizes the businesses. \par
\par
Council President Bethea commented on alcoholic usage downtown.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer asked if Council has to address every liquor license application.\par
\par
City Manager Pete Lee responded staff could present an ordinance change if Council wished.\par
\par
Council Pro Tem Musleh stated he would be in agreement to remove these from direct Council approval, noting Council can step in to revoke a license if need be.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty expressed concern about staff having the power to make those decisions.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer also asked for some filtering when noting calls for service at an address, noting this item stated 38 calls for service, but half of those calls were routine police check ins.\par
\par
With no further discussion, the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Mayor Marciano thanked the speakers who shared their kratom\u8209?related experiences and stressed that kratom has become a serious and growing public safety concern in Ocala. He referenced medical cases, overdose incidents, and rising reports received over recent months, noting that several states-and even California-have already banned kratom. He emphasized that statewide action may eventually come but urged the city not to wait. He proposed partnering with Marion County to draft and adopt an ordinance banning the sale of kratom locally and noted that preliminary work with the county attorney has already begun.\par
\par
City Attorney Sexton stated that he has coordinated with Marion County attorney\rquote s office, which is prepared to move forward with its own kratom ordinance. He explained that Ocala can collaborate with the county to adopt a similar ordinance or tailor one based on Council feedback. He noted that few jurisdictions have enacted such bans but said potential legal issues can be addressed, and requested direction from the Council on how they wish to proceed.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield emphasized the seriousness of kratom\rquote s risks, stating that the city should take a clear stance and pursue whatever legal measures are available to restrict or eliminate its sale. He urged stronger standards for sellers and action to protect young people, noting that the product appears deceptively harmless. Council Member Dreyer sought clarification on the proposed ban and confirmed that enforcement could be handled through code enforcement, supported by law enforcement as needed. Mayor Marciano confirmed the County's intention to use their code enforcement officers. Council Member Dreyer noted speaking with Chief Balken; OPD is on board with enforcement.\par
\par
City Attorney Sexton noted potential legal concerns, explaining that a local kratom ban could be viewed as stricter than what state law (Senate Bill 180) allows. He said he has not yet discussed with county counsel how their draft ordinance addresses this issue but plans to do so. He added that the law provides some flexibility to revise regulations if challenged without incurring additional penalties. Sexton advised that these concerns can be worked through during drafting and that the Council will have the opportunity to reconsider its approach if a legal challenge arises.\par
\par
Mayor Marciano discussed the various forms the product can come in. Council Member Mansfield highlighted the lack of regulations and testing available to verify what is in any of the products, noting the medical marijuana won't touch the product. He stated the City needs an ordinance.\par
\par
Council President Bethea stated the City should not blindly copy the County's ordinance.\par
\par
Council Pro Tem Musleh questioned whether it would be classified as a code violation or a criminal violation? If code, would that make the Code Enforcement Board the arbiter, or the Special Magistrate? If the Code Board, they will require education on the subject. He further questioned whether advertising would be a violation.\par
\par
Mr. Sexton confirmed the intention would be to make the marketing and selling of kratom illegal. The current law states it is illegal to sell to anyone under 21. The proposed County version would empower the County to remove the certificate of occupancy of a business, effectively shutting down the business. The City may consider that law enforcement would be more appropriate.\par
\par
Council Members Dreyer and Musleh agreed. Pro Tem Musleh noted a code violation allows for the City to levy fines, follow repeat offenders, and revoke occupancy certificates.\par
\par
City Manager Lee commented that the DEA has, within the last week, issued an emergency notice regarding the 7-OH version of kratom, placing it into Schedule One drugs.\par
\par
Mayor Marciano noted that 7-OH is only one compound and there are many other derivatives.\par
\par
Mr. Sexton explained the problem remains that there are many derivatives of kratom, and one of the pitfalls of traditional methodology allows for loopholes. The County's ordinance very broadly defines kratom and doesn't limit it to specific variations being regulated or prohibited. He noted he has his direction from Council.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Clay Albright, representing Rock Homes, requested relief from substantial code enforcement fines related to tree removal and site improvements on a property under development. He explained that his client acted in good faith based on guidance from staff and engineers, but later received unexpected citations and daily fines due to miscommunication and notices sent to an incorrect address. He asked Council for assistance in resolving the issue ahead of an upcoming property closing.\par
\par
City Manager Pete Lee noted he had informed Mr. Albright prior to the meeting that he cannot undo the decision of the Code Enforcement Board or Special Magistrate. He further noted the City has not received a restoration plan nor site plan.\par
\par
Growth Management Director Jeff Shrum stated he has received a text from the Code Enforcement manager; there's been an agreement on cross attachment release that requires prosecution fees to be paid.\par
\par
Mr. Albright expressed strong frustration with the city\rquote s code enforcement process, stating that in his experience the department often acts arrogantly and provides no meaningful avenue for citizens to question or resolve issues. He urged the council to establish an oversight body to ensure accountability, noting that while some violations are justified, many are unreasonable and difficult to discuss or resolve with current staff. He emphasized that the public is increasingly discouraged by these interactions.\par
\par
Mr. Lee explained that, as he understands it, the delay in resolving the code issue stems from the engineer awaiting a required survey before submitting the updated site plan. He noted the removed trees were old, declining, and consistent with the site plan\rquote s long\u8209?term needs. He outlined how the restoration plan and new parking lot design are expected to address the violation. There had been 2 hearings, one in April and one in June, and he stated Mr. Albright denied knowledge of the second hearing due to an incorrect address on the notice. He further stated the city will return to the Code Enforcement Board to request elimination of the accrued fines once the updated plans are submitted.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer urged the city to make code enforcement less punitive, noting that serious violations should be addressed but homeowners and businesses improving their properties should not face excessive penalties. She highlighted inconsistencies in enforcement and said this was the third code\u8209?related complaint she had heard in a week, emphasizing the need for a more reasonable and consistent approach.\par
\par
Mr. Lee agreed, but noted in this case, the site originally had trees and upon a follow-up inspection there were no trees on the site, with no permits pulled. Mr. Albright stated the trees were removed because they were dead or dying and they considered them a threat to cars and patients. Council Member Dreyer questioned if the tree removal permits would have been granted; Mr. Lee affirmed they would have. \par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Chief Planning Official Endira Madraveren explained that the current community business zoning is not permitted under the neighborhood future land use designation. The applicant seeks to change the designation from neighborhood to low intensity to align it with the existing zoning and ensure consistency between the Comprehensive Plan and land development regulations. She noted that all three parcels were annexed in 1975, two are developed with commercial uses, and one remains undeveloped. The proposed low intensity category allows higher density and intensity than the existing neighborhood designation and supports the established commercial corridor and surrounding development patterns. The Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended approval, staff supports the request.\par
\par
Agent Tim Haynes explained that the proposed future land use change, together with recent City of Ocala adjustments, aligns the Comprehensive Plan and zoning with current on\u8209?site conditions. He noted that two of the three parcels continued operating commercially despite a prior neighborhood designation and are now under contract by the owner of the westernmost commercial parcels. Haynes emphasized that the area is already within an established commercial corridor behind the Gateway Plaza, with adjacent county property used for drainage. He added that a related upcoming request includes down\u8209?zoning the rear portion of the property to institutional for a planned school, creating a natural transition from commercial to residential areas. He reported that the neighborhood has agreed to future use of open fields for a sports complex and that an agreement is recorded. Haynes stated that local business operators and adjacent owners support the transition due to the positive changes underway and noted he was available for questions.\line\line Representative of \f1 Z & T Partners, LLC, \f0 Todd DeRegnaucourt, who also serves as principal of Capstone Academy located on one of the subject parcels, stated that the school moved into a building that had significantly deteriorated and has since invested substantial funds in renovations. He noted that Z&T Partners now has the adjacent health spa parcel under contract, which also requires major rehabilitation, and plans to invest further in improvements that will create approximately 30 professional jobs. He added that the rear parcel is planned for development as a sports complex with open fields, providing a buffer for nearby neighborhoods. He thanked the council for the opportunity to speak, and no questions were raised.\par
\par
A resident of La Jolla, newly returned to Ocala, expressed strong support for the proposed zoning changes, noting that the area has long been inconsistent and patchwork in its development. She stated that recent improvements to the nearby plaza have been dramatic and that aligning the zoning to allow continued growth-particularly with Capstone\rquote s involvement-will benefit the neighborhood. She emphasized that she and her husband chose to make La Jolla their home again and believe the proposed changes will positively support the community\rquote s future.\par
\par
Business owner Caroline Miller, who has operated the Ocala Bicycle Center at the site for 21 years, also spoke in favor. She explained that under the new ownership, significant repairs and upgrades have been completed, including roofing, lighting, landscaping, security cameras, and regular maintenance-far more than in prior years. She said these improvements have greatly enhanced safety and appearance for both customers and employees. Miller noted she looks forward to continued positive collaboration with Capstone as they expand operations.\par
\par
Austin Burger, a longtime Ocala resident and business owner in the plaza, stated that conditions have significantly improved since the current ownership took over two years ago. He highlighted enhanced lighting, regular AC maintenance, prompt communication, quick responses to issues, and overall cleaner, more presentable facilities. He noted that these improvements directly benefit his comic business as well as other neighboring businesses and expressed support for approval of the request.\par
\par
There being no further discussion the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\par
}
