\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Budget Director Tammi Haslam presented the proposed Fiscal Year 2026-27 budget, totaling $1,269,705,929, and outlined key dates for upcoming public hearings and approvals. She highlighted major drivers of the $116.8 million overall increase, including higher pension costs, electric utility expenses, general fund needs, and sanitation costs. The general fund budget of $207,375,596 is balanced at the current millage rate of 6.6177, with ad valorem revenue increases due to rising taxable values and no changes to fire assessment rates or enterprise fund transfers. Ms. Haslam reviewed planned capital improvement projects totaling about $71.2 million across 48 projects, covering infrastructure, facilities, fleet, IT, recreation, and water resources. All enterprise funds are balanced and meeting reserve requirements. She noted continued pressures from rising salary, benefit, and operational costs, potential impacts of upcoming property tax reform, and new reporting requirements under House Bill 1329. Ms. Haslam concluded by expressing appreciation for Council, staff, and leadership support.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer asked whether the city had determined if the local business tax could be eliminated, noting that the budget still showed revenue from it. Ms. Haslam responded that staff had completed their review and would bring the item to Council shortly, and that the budget line could be updated once a final determination is made. Council Member Dreyer also questioned the inclusion of a $500,000 roundabout project at South 18th Avenue, stating it was not part of the city\rquote s prioritized road improvements. City Manager Pete Lee agreed and explained that southeast area projects were being reevaluated, with a report to be brought back to Council and the roundabout likely removed or reallocated. Council Member Dreyer expressed concern over the city\rquote s continued funding of nonprofit agencies, asserting that taxpayer dollars should remain focused on core public purposes such as safety, education, infrastructure, and natural resources, and suggesting that funding nonprofits through property taxes is inappropriate without voter approval through a dedicated ballot initiative.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield agreed with Council Member Dreyer\rquote s concerns, noting that with anticipated state-level changes, the city should prepare for tighter financial conditions. He suggested reevaluating planned hires and certain capital and building expenditures, emphasizing a need to \ldblquote tighten belts\rdblquote and operate more leanly to avoid future budget strain. Mansfield also questioned projects that residents had expressed opposition to and encouraged a full review of items he had flagged.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty echoed concerns about nonprofit funding and described how the process had shifted over the years-from Council selecting recipients directly to staff managing recommendations. He noted that some nonprofits receive multiple forms of city support and stated he was willing to forgo funding even for an organization on whose board he serves, arguing the current process is flawed and should be reexamined.\par
\par
City Manager Pete Lee clarified that nonprofit allocations remain entirely at Council\rquote s discretion, explaining that the groups listed are those Council initially chose and kept in place. He described previous attempts to consolidate funding through the Community Foundation, which did not work as intended, and reaffirmed that Council may continue, modify, or discontinue nonprofit funding as it sees fit.\par
\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Airport Director Matt Grow explained that Ocala will host a new airshow event beginning with the inaugural show on April 30, followed by additional spring events in 2028 and 2029. He noted that JLC Airshow Management, an experienced producer of airshows across the Southeast, will handle nearly all aspects of event operations, including vendors, sanitation, fencing, insurance, parking, shuttles, and traffic management. He also highlighted a proposed $100,000 sponsorship from the Tourist Development Council, subject to approval. The agreement includes revenue\u8209?sharing provisions and allows either party to cancel with 60 days\rquote notice. Grow emphasized that the event is a valuable opportunity to showcase the airport and attract up to 45,000 visitors, generating significant economic activity. He noted that the Airport Advisory Board fully supports the event and staff recommends approval.\par

Council Member Dreyer emphasized that the funding for associated police and fire services comes from airport-generated revenue rather than taxpayer dollars. \par
\par
Corey Lock of the Marion County Visitor\rquote s Center explained that the projected attendance and economic impacts are conservative estimates and highlighted his experience in the aerospace industry, noting that Blue Angels shows draw large crowds. He added that efforts to secure the Blue Angels began in 2022, and they were successfully confirmed for the first two years, with hopes for additional future appearances.\par

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}}
{\colortbl ;\red128\green128\blue128;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 City Clerk Jacobs announced the name of the taxing authority is the City of Ocala. Fiscal year 2026-27 operating millage rate is 6.6177, which is greater than the rollback rate of 6.3727 by 3.84%. Ad valorem tax revenues are increasing to support the addition of critical employees and assist with increasing cost pressures related to salary, benefits, and operating costs.\par
\par
Ms. Lauren DiOrio, CEO of the Community Foundation, addressed the proposed changes to nonprofit funding, clarifying that the Community Foundation does not retain an administrative fee from City of Ocala funds and that all funds are passed through to support nonprofit services. She referenced a position paper provided to the Council outlining recommendations for improving the nonprofit funding selection process and emphasized that existing state guidelines provide a sound framework for community investment. Ms. DiOrio expressed support for developing a transparent process aligned with the City's goals and highlighted the important role local nonprofits play in serving community needs. She also invited Council members to participate in the upcoming Give4Marion celebration.\par
\par
Mayor Marciano thanked Ms. DiOrio and the local nonprofits for their service to the community, noting the increasing number of requests for assistance he receives from residents in need. He stated that City support for nonprofits helps address community needs and provides valuable resources for residents. The Mayor expressed support for establishing a clear and accountable funding process while emphasizing that nonprofit organizations provide significant benefits and a strong return on the City's investment.\par
\par
Council Pro Tem Musleh echoed Mayor Marciano's comments and commended Ms. DiOrio bringing the position paper to Council's attention.\par
\par
Wayne Little Jr., representing the MLK Commemorative Committee, thanked the City for its longstanding support and highlighted the committee's contributions to the community, including awarding approximately $100,000 in scholarships to more than 175 students since 2000. He noted that City funding helps support scholarships, youth programs, and annual MLK observance events, and stated that the proposed loss of $10,000 in funding would create challenges for the volunteer-led organization. Mr. Little respectfully requested that the Council consider options such as partial funding, matching contributions, or continued in-kind City services to help sustain the committee's programs and events.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer requested that staff compile a comprehensive report of all City support provided to nonprofit organizations, including direct funding, in-kind services, discounted leases, and public safety support, to give the Council a complete picture of its contributions. She suggested holding the nonprofit funding allocation until a more formal process could be developed.\par
\par
City Manager Pete Lee agreed to provide the information and stated that staff could also develop formal agreements with nonprofits that include documented expectations and performance measures. He recommended bringing all nonprofit funding agreements back to the Council together for review.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty and Council Member Bethea suggested proceeding with the nonprofit funding allocations as originally included in the current budget while staff develops a revised process for future years, noting that several organizations rely on the funding.\par
\par
Council President Pro Tem Musleh supported providing the funding this year and using the coming year to develop a more comprehensive process, including consideration of all direct and in-kind support provided by the City.\par
\par
Budget Director Tammi Haslam explained that no budget resolution would be required if the funds remained within the operating budget and were simply reallocated.\par
\par
The Council reached a consensus to proceed with the nonprofit funding as originally budgeted for the current fiscal year while directing staff to compile a report on all nonprofit support and develop proposed agreements and performance measures for future funding consideration.\par
\par
There being no further discussion the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\par
Council President Bethea announced the time of adoption at 5:30pm.\par
\par
Clerk Jacobs announced the tentative fiscal year 2026-27 general fund budget is $207,375,596, and the City's total tentative fiscal year 2026-27 budget is $1,269,705,929.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Clay Albright expressed concerns about leadership within the City of Ocala, comparing recent issues to a lack of accountability seen in a sports context. He stated that the city\rquote s code enforcement department has developed a problematic culture that is causing fear and frustration in the business community, citing his own experience with repeated citations he believes to be retaliatory. Mr. Albright urged the council to address these issues before renewing the City Manager\rquote s contract, arguing that ongoing problems within the department reflect broader leadership failures and should be resolved prior to extending that agreement.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty expressed concern over the city manager receiving an \ldblquote exceeds expectations\rdblquote review despite ongoing issues he believes reflect weak leadership and poor responsiveness. He noted repeated delays in getting answers to councilmember requests and pointed to downtown business closures and unresolved concerns raised by affected business owners. Council Member Hilty stated that effective leadership is not being demonstrated and suggested exploring new leadership options to keep pace with Ocala\rquote s growth.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield stated that while he agrees improvements are needed in certain divisions, particularly Code Enforcement, he believes Mr. Lee is performing well overall and shows strong leadership. Mr. Mansfield acknowledged departmental problems and said he has personally worked with the city manager on needed changes, emphasizing that issues caused by individual employees should not be equated with poor management. He cited positive feedback from contractors and expressed full support for the Mr. Lee.\par
\par
Mr. Hilty rebutted that many concerns involve lack of responsiveness directly from the city manager, not just departmental staff. He noted that community members fear retribution and are hesitant to speak up, reinforcing his belief that leadership shortcomings are broader and more significant than Mr. Mansfield suggested.\par
\par
Council Pro Tem Musleh stated strong support for the Mr. Lee, noting his own previous experience with serving on the Code Enforcement Board and acknowledging it is a difficult, often unpopular function. He agreed that the department currently has issues and likely had the wrong person in a key role, but said the city manager has already recognized this and is working to correct it. Mr. Musleh emphasized he has not heard complaints about the city manager\rquote s overall performance, supported taking action on the long\u8209?delayed Hilton matter, and cautioned against frequently replacing city managers. He concluded that the city manager has earned a contract extension.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer explained that she addresses concerns directly with the city manager rather than saving them for evaluations, so nothing in his review should be a surprise. She emphasized the importance of balancing criticism with recognition of the many positive developments happening citywide. Ms. Dreyer noted that Growth Management is historically a challenging and often\u8209?criticized department regardless of leadership, yet contractors report that working with the City is better now than ever. While agreeing that Code Enforcement needs refinement, she cautioned against focusing solely on problems and urged the council to also acknowledge the broader successes throughout the organization.\par
\par
Mayor Marciano emphasized the importance of maintaining the city\rquote s appearance but noted that everyone, including himself, has faults. He stated that the city manager\rquote s role is to lead and build a healthy organizational culture, and he sees that leadership reflected in how hard employees work for him. The Mayor acknowledged issues within Code Enforcement but said Mr. Lee has acted to address them and is committed to improvement. He warned against \ldblquote Monday\u8209?morning quarterbacking\rdblquote and assuming leadership is better elsewhere, asserting that the City already has a strong leader in the current city manager, who he believes deserves to continue in the role.\par
\par
There being no further discussion the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Mr. Guinn requested an update on the status of the Ocala Fiber expansion, asked whether the previously discussed $46 million bond financing plan remained in place, and inquired about the availability of a fiber coverage map, noting continued interest from a potential buyer in evaluating the system.\par
\par
Chief Financial Officer Janice Mitchell responded that Ocala Fiber continues to expand service, with current construction occurring in the Dearman area. She stated that the anticipated financing plan is being reevaluated and is expected to be less than $46 million once system-wide design and cost estimates are completed. Ms. Mitchell also advised that detailed fiber infrastructure maps are not publicly available due to critical infrastructure and security considerations. Discussion also noted that any future consideration of a sale would be a Council decision and that the utility's growth could affect its valuation.\par
\par
Council members discussed whether to revisit previous proposals related to Ocala Fiber. Council Member Musleh stated he was not interested in reopening discussions that had already been considered the previous year. Council Member Hilty said any consideration of the issue would require a more thorough workshop discussion. Council Member Dreyer noted that Ocala Fiber may become increasingly important as a revenue-generating asset for the City and said it was premature to discuss a sale before the system is fully built out and its costs are better defined.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield expressed interest in receiving a clearer long-term plan for Ocala Fiber, including goals, growth strategy, and implementation timelines. In response, Ms. Mitchell committed to providing regular updates on system expansion, including conduit installation, customer connections, and operational improvements.\par
\par
Ms. Mitchell further explained that Ocala Fiber continues to grow in a competitive market, generates revenue for the City's general fund, and faces challenges associated with upgrading and expanding a network that was not originally designed to operate as a retail internet service provider. Staff emphasized that the utility remains financially stable and retains significant value as a municipal asset.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Ms. Baillie presented an overview of the Marion Cultural Alliance\rquote s 25\u8209?year history and current impact. She explained that the organization was founded in 2001 following the Horse Fever public art project and is now recognized by the City of Ocala as the lead arts agency. Ms. Baillie highlighted the continued presence of Horse Fever sculptures throughout the community and noted recent additions created through the Art in Business program. She reported key impact statistics, including hundreds of thousands of residents and visitors served, over $700,000 in grants awarded to arts organizations, and significant economic impact as measured by Americans for the Arts.\par
\par
Ms. Baillie also summarized funding partnerships such as the National Endowment for the Arts and the Four Friends grants, as well as scholarship support for local students. She provided an annual report for Brick City Center for the Arts, emphasizing monthly exhibits, community programming, strong visitor numbers, and frequent gallery rentals. She encouraged use of the Ocala Metro Arts Scene as a comprehensive listing of cultural events.\par
\par
Finally, Ms. Baillie outlined MCA\rquote s upcoming three\u8209?year strategic plan, including expanded grantmaking, strengthened partnerships, creation of an Ocala Art Trail app, and collaboration with the Visitor and Convention Bureau to promote downtown Ocala as an arts destination.\par
\par
Council President Bethea commended Ms. Baillie and the MCA for all the work they do within the community.\par
\par
}

minutes_note:

{\colortbl ;\red128\green128\blue128;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Council Member Hilty expressed concern that the TECO franchise agreement had expired four years earlier and had not been renewed, questioning the City's continued collection of franchise fees without an updated agreement and raising concerns about potential liability and lack of transparency.\par
\par
City Attorney Sexton stated that the delay was primarily the result of contract negotiations handled by his office rather than the City Manager. He explained that the agreement remained enforceable because both parties continued to perform under its terms, with TECO continuing operations and franchise fee payments and the City continuing to allow use of its rights-of-way. He stated that the City had not suffered any known financial loss or harm as a result of the delay.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty maintained that the agreement should have been renewed sooner and emphasized the need for better communication and transparency with the Council regarding such matters. Mr. Sexton acknowledged that the process took longer than it should have but reiterated that the delay was related to ongoing negotiations.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer stated that she shared concerns regarding the expired agreement and questioned why the City did not have an electronic system for tracking contract expiration dates. She noted that the review of legacy contracts may identify additional agreements that have expired while continuing to be honored. Council Member Dreyer stated that staff had indicated a contract database was being developed to improve contract monitoring and emphasized the importance of proactively tracking contracts before expiration.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty expressed concern that contracts involving significant financial amounts could go unnoticed and stated that the Council had not been informed of the issue. Council Member Dreyer responded that the situation appeared to be the result of increased workloads, rapid growth, and the need to modernize policies and procedures rather than any intentional wrongdoing. She suggested the City review and strengthen its processes for contract management and related administrative functions.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty also noted that turnover among leadership and department directors can create challenges. Council Member Dreyer acknowledged that leadership transitions can affect operations but stated that such changes occur regularly in organizations and highlighted the importance of having strong systems and procedures in place.\par
\par
Council President Bethea acknowledged Council Member Hilty's concerns and stated that he also agreed with Council Member Dreyer's comments regarding the need for improved contract tracking and management processes. He noted that staff are working in a fast-paced environment and emphasized the importance of addressing operational issues as they arise.\par
\par
Council President Bethea expressed support for exploring electronic tools or software to monitor contract expiration dates and stated that the Council should support staff in implementing solutions, including providing necessary funding if additional resources are required. He emphasized the importance of balancing organizational needs while strengthening administrative processes and thanked both Council Members Hilty and Dreyer for raising their concerns.\par
\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Fleet Director John King presented a request for approval of an additional expenditure of $190,936 related to the purchase of fire apparatus for Ocala Fire Rescue. He explained that during a prior Council-approved purchase for fire department capital equipment, a prepayment discount from the vendor had been included in the project cost assumptions. Following internal discussions regarding the City's prepayment practices and associated financial and contractual risks, the anticipated prepayment was not made.\par
\par
Mr. King stated that he mistakenly applied the revised approach to an existing approved purchase rather than to future transactions. He noted that the City retained the purchase funds and earned interest income, and when combined with credits received from the vendor, the financial benefit exceeded the value of the forfeited prepayment discount. Mr. King accepted responsibility for the oversight and requested Council approval of the additional funding needed to complete the purchase.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty asked for clarification on the $56,000 credit toward future trucks provided by Matheny Motors E1. Would the City lose out on the credit if future trucks were purchased from another company? Mr. King explained that Matheny Motors E1 is a on a state contract, and thus is already competitively sourced. Mr. Hilty expressed concern the City would be locked into purchasing more equipment from Matheny. Mr. King further explained some of the credit will be applied toward proposed CIP purchases that will be presented at the next council meeting, and some discounts have been applied to other purchases already as well.\par
\par
Council Member Hilty referenced an email he received October 14 that outlined an issue with the receiving process when these trucks had been received on October 2. He expressed frustration that Council was not informed of the mix-up when it happened, and that what he understood from City Manager Pete Lee yesterday differed from Mr. King's explanation of events. Mr. Lee disputed this characterization, noting a staff member made a mistake that was rectified. Mr. Hilty questioned how many mistakes happen that they don't hear about.\par
\par
Council President Bethea asked if the City lost anything with this error. Mr. King replied the City stands to gain approximately $127, with the interest earned from the overpayment monies held in an interest-bearing account and the $56,000 purchase credit.\par
\par
Mr. Lee stated Matheny has been nothing but gracious and cooperative with staff. He explained his understanding of events, noting verification in emails. He further stated he takes responsibility for staff, and commented that his first step upon finding out about an issue is to fix it.\par
\par
Council Member Mansfield commented that mistakes are inevitable in an organization of the City's size and complexity. He emphasized that the focus should be on how staff and leadership respond to and correct mistakes rather than on the mistakes themselves. He expressed confidence that the error was unintentional, acknowledged Mr. King's willingness to take responsibility, and stated that continuous improvement and accountability are the appropriate measures of performance.\par
\par
Council Member Dreyer thanked staff for taking responsibility and stated that the explanation provided was reasonable. She emphasized the importance of fully vetting agenda items and refining internal processes before they come before Council to avoid confusion and public misunderstanding. During discussion of a recently delivered rescue vehicle, she questioned how procedural failures occurred and encouraged additional safeguards and checklists to ensure compliance with established procedures.\par
\par
Mr. King explained that a rescue vehicle had been delivered and placed into service without the required title documentation, contrary to established procedures. Once the issue was discovered, the vehicle was promptly removed from service until the necessary documentation was received. He noted that written procedures and cross-departmental review processes are in place but agreed that additional refinements and streamlining may be beneficial as the organization grows.\par
\par
There being no further discussion the motion carried by roll call vote.\par
\par
}
